papers.title_in_file: A quantum graph approach to metamaterial design
papers.version_note: The text layer is the Scientific Reports 2022 published version (volume 12, article 18006, received 7 July 2022, accepted 12 October 2022); the file name and record id carry 2023 and arXiv 2306.05890.
papers.what_it_is: A theory and numerical-demonstration paper that models a 2D metamaterial as an infinite square periodic quantum graph with open-graph resonators at the vertices, and computes band diagrams, Gaussian beam refraction at one interface and an N layer transfer matrix.
papers.why_not: The paper uses quantum graph scattering theory as a classical wave model of metamaterials; it has no quantum computing or machine learning workload and no fraud, finance or evaluation content. Entries below are filed under method as the modelling approach.

assertions.value: The authors state that the metamaterial is modeled as an infinite square periodic quantum graph embedded in a 2D real space, with a single resonant element modelled as an open quantum graph that is then periodically arranged.
assertions.anchor: Introduction and Section 'Waves in finite open quantum graphs', p.2
quotes: the metamaterial is modeled as an infinite square periodic quantum graph embedded in a 2D real space.
we can model a single resonant element as an open quantum graph, which is then periodically arranged to construct the metamaterial.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own model set-up in the Introduction and in the resonator section.

assertions.value: The authors state that the mapping from incoming to outgoing wave amplitudes at the vertices is described by a unitary matrix, and that they assume Neumann boundary conditions at individual vertices, enforcing wave continuity and flux conservation.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Waves in finite open quantum graphs', p.3
quotes: the mapping from all incoming to all outgoing wave amplitudes at the vertices is described by a unitary matrix
We assume Neumann boundary conditions at individual vertices enforcing wave continuity and flux conservation at each
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its vertex model in the resonator section.
assertions.reader_inference: A unitary vertex matrix means the model has no loss or absorption; the paper does not discuss loss.

assertions.value: The authors give the scattering matrix of a connected open graph, reducing it to a single scatterer, as SˆŴ(k) = SˆLL + SˆLE Iˆ − Pˆ (k)SˆEE −1Pˆ (k)SˆEL, built from prompt lead reflections, lead to edge coupling, edge propagation and edge to lead coupling.
assertions.anchor: Eq. (6), Section 'Waves in finite open quantum graphs', p.3
quotes: SˆŴ(k) = SˆLL + SˆLE Iˆ − Pˆ (k)SˆEE −1Pˆ (k)SˆEL,
reducing the entire connected graph in Ŵ(V , E, L) to a single scatterer illustrated in Fig. 2.
assertions.certainty_reason: The text points to Kottos and Smilansky for details; the derivation is not given in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The expression is the standard graph scattering formula attributed to reference 17 in the text.

assertions.value: The authors state that Bloch's theorem relates the solution in any unit cell to the solution at the central vertex, and that the wave vector k on each edge and the quasi-wave vectors fulfill the secular equation det Iˆ − eiklBˆ (κx, κy)SˆŴ(k) = 0.
assertions.anchor: Eq. (11) and Eq. (15), Section 'A quantum graph model for a metamaterial', pp.4-5
quotes: we can use Bloch’s theorem to describe the wave solution in any unit cell nm in terms of the solution at the central vertex
which is satisfied if the wave vector k on each edge and the quasi-wave vectors κx and κy fulfill the secular equation
det Iˆ − eiklBˆ (κx, κy)SˆŴ(k) = 0.
assertions.certainty_reason: The condition is stated as the paper's dispersion condition, derived in the text from Eqs. (9), (10) and (12).

assertions.value: The authors state that real or imaginary solutions of the Bloch wave number correspond to propagating or evanescent waves respectively, the latter occurring in band gaps.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Wave solutions for the infinite lattice', p.5
quotes: We encounter real or imaginary solutions of κx(k, κy) corresponding to propagating or evanescent waves, respectively, the latter occurring in band gaps.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement of how the paper interprets its dispersion solutions.

assertions.value: For a lattice without resonators, where each edge is directly connected through a point-scatterer vertex, the authors give the dispersion relation 2 cos (kl) = cos (κxl) + cos (κyl).
assertions.anchor: Eq. (18), Section 'Wave propagation in metamaterials, plane wave solutions', p.5
quotes: we consider a lattice without resonators where each edge is directly connected through the vertex.
2 cos (kl) = cos (κxl) + cos (κyl).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the result 'by solving Eq. (15)' without showing the algebra, so the derivation is not quotable.

assertions.value: The authors state that the energy flow is given by the Poynting vector normal to the iso-frequency contour, and that plane wave solutions travel in the direction of the wave vector, which does not necessarily agree with the direction of energy flow.
assertions.anchor: Sections on plane wave solutions and Gaussian beams, pp.5-6
quotes: energy flow is given by the Poynting vector J = (Jx, Jy)T normal to the iso-frequency contour.
Plane wave solutions travel in the direction of the wave vector κ , which does not necessarily agree with the direction of energy flow given by the Poynting
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines its energy flow direction this way in the plane wave section.

assertions.value: The authors give the one dimensional flux of the wave function on edge p as k times the difference between the squared magnitudes of the outgoing and incoming amplitudes on that edge.
quotes: The 1D flux J of the wave function ψnm
assertions.certainty_reason: The flux is the paper's own definition used to build the Poynting vector.

assertions.value: The authors construct a Gaussian beam by Fourier expansion over the eigenfunctions on the iso-frequency contour, with the beam width and a phase factor setting the width and tilt of the beam; solutions outside the contour are evanescent and contribute nothing in the far field. Space on the graph is discretised, so the spatial integrals are too.
assertions.anchor: Eqs. (22) to (24), Section 'Wave propagation in metamaterials, Gaussian beams', pp.6-7
quotes: Solutions outside are evanescent and so contribute nothing in the far field.
We chose the beam profile to be Gaussian
determines the tilt angle of the beam with respect to the horizontal axis of the lattice.
Since the space on the graph is discretised, so too are the spacial integrals.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its beam construction and discretisation as method set-up.

assertions.value: The authors report that varying the phase modulation across each resonant element in only one dimension breaks the symmetry of the scattering and gives a saddle shaped band, which they state can be exploited for negative refraction; the figure caption gives lx = 1 and ly = 1 for the symmetric case and lx = 0 and ly = 1 for the asymmetric case.
quotes: varying the phase modulation across each resonant element only in one dimension breaks the symmetry of the scattering and gives rise to a saddle shaped band, which can be exploited to yield negative refraction
Plot (b) is for lx = 1 , ly = 1 . Plot (c) is for lx = 0 , ly = 1.
assertions.certainty_reason: A numerical band diagram for one resonator design, shown only as a figure; the text gives no further quantitative detail.
assertions.reader_inference: The result is for a single cross resonator family at the parameter values named in the caption.

assertions.value: The authors state that the two materials share the single value of k and the Bloch phase tangential to the interface, giving the boundary condition that the tangential Bloch wave numbers of material 1 and 2 are equal; the wave vectors normal to the interface follow from the dispersion curve of each material.
quotes: enforcing k1 = k2 := k
leading to the boundary condition κ1,y = κ2,y := κy
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states these as the boundary conditions of its interface model.

assertions.value: The authors state that with the eigenfunctions rescaled so the horizontal flux magnitude of each component is equal, flux conservation across the interface reduces to |A1|2 + |B2|2 = |B1|2 + |A2|2, meaning the sum of the squared magnitudes of A1 and B2 equals that of B1 and A2, so interface scattering is described as a unitary process.
quotes: we rescale the eigenfunction solutions of each material such that the magnitude of the horizontal flux of each component is equal
and wave scattering at the interface can then be described in terms of a unitary scattering process.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated in the interface section as following from the flux scaling choice; the scaling assumes real normal Bloch wave numbers (propagating waves), which the paper notes next to Eq. (29).
assertions.reader_inference: The unitarity holds for propagating (real normal wave number) channels; the paper does not treat evanescent channels at the interface.

assertions.value: The authors define the interface scattering matrix by two events: event I is a wave incident from material 1 onto material 2 with amplitude A1 = 1 and B2 = 0, and event II is a wave incident from material 2 onto material 1 with amplitude B2 = 1 and A1 = 0, each giving a reflected and a transmitted amplitude.
quotes: Event I describes a wave incident from material 1 onto material 2 with amplitude A1 = 1 and B2 = 0
Event II describes a wave incident from material 2 onto material 1 with amplitude B2 = 1 and A1 = 0
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines its interface scattering matrix by these two events.

assertions.value: The authors show, as numerical figures, a Gaussian beam incident from material 1 with amplitude A1 = 1 and no incident beam from material 2, with B2 = 0, onto an interface, with beam focal point n′ = −60 and tilt κy′ = 1/l; with the saddle shaped band material on the right they report the reflection and transmission behaviour of Fig. 11. The text gives no numerical refraction angles or coefficients.
assertions.anchor: Eq. (40), Figs. 10 and 11, p.10 and p.11
quotes: The results of this unitary interface scattering is shown in Fig. 10 for a Gaussian beam incident from material 1 with amplitude A1 = 1 and no incident beam from material 2, that is, B2 = 0.
The expansion coefficients α−60 are as in Eq. (23) for a beam focal point n′ = −60 and tilt given by κy′ = 1/l.
one obtains the reflection/transmission behaviour shown in Fig. 11.
assertions.certainty_reason: A single numerical run shown as a figure; the results are in the images, not the text.
assertions.reader_inference: The negative refraction and beam steering named in the abstract rest on these figures; the text layer holds no numbers for them.

assertions.value: The authors state that the coefficients for N layered metamaterials are found by the Transfer Matrix Method, which expresses the wave amplitudes in material N in terms of those in material 1 and can be rearranged so the whole layered system acts as a single point scatterer.
assertions.anchor: Eqs. (41) to (46), Section 'Waves in N layered metamaterials', p.12
quotes: This is done by the Transfer Matrix
Having now formulated both scattering and propagation, one can express the wave amplitudes in material N in terms of the wave amplitudes in material 1.
such that the entire system of layered materials acts as a single point scatterer
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines its N layer formalism in this section.

assertions.value: The authors show a three layered example of three metamaterials whose scattering matrices are the point scatterer, the cross resonator with parameters 0 and 4.45, and the point scatterer again, at k = 1/l, with an incident wave of amplitude A1 = 1 from the first material and no incident wave from the last. The result is given only as a figure.
quotes: iso-frequency contours of three metamaterials with properties defined by scattering matrices
SˆŴcross (k; 0, 4.45) and SˆŴpoint for k = 1/l
assertions.certainty_reason: A single numerical illustration reported only in a figure.

assertions.value: The authors state that existing simulation techniques for metamaterials can be quite time consuming when setting up the models, let alone considering design modifications, and that simple and computationally cheap models are needed for proof of principle studies.
quotes: These simulation techniques can be quite time consuming when setting up the models, let alone considering design modifications
need for simple and computationally cheap models for proof of principle studies.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim without a timing comparison in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper reports no runtime or cost measurement for its own method or for the finite element, boundary element or transmission line models.

assertions.value: The authors propose a graph based technique that they describe as allowing a fast and flexible way to test resonant element proposals embedded periodically within a 2D square lattice, and state that the computation reduces to low-dimensional matrix problems with the help of Bloch's theorem.
quotes: We propose here a graph based technique for designing metamaterials allowing for a fast and flexible way to test resonant element proposals embedded periodically within a 2D square lattice.
the computation can be reduced to low-dimensional matrix problems with the help of Bloch’s theorem.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim of speed and flexibility; no benchmark is reported.

assertions.value: The authors state that a generalisation to 3D is straightforward by adding additional edges and vertices in the extra dimension. The paper does not carry out a three dimensional calculation.
quotes: A generalisation to 3D is straightforward by adding additional edges and vertices in the extra dimension.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim with no 3D result in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that further results modelling various special wave effects will be presented in forthcoming publications, and that the datasets and the code used for the study are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request. The paper includes no public code or data link.
assertions.anchor: Conclusion p.12; Data availability and Code availability, p.13
quotes: Further results modelling various special wave effects will be presented in forthcoming publications.
The code used to generate the datasets shown in this study are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own scope limit and availability terms.

assertions.value: The authors attribute to Veselago the result that a material with both permittivity and permeability less than zero has a negative refractive index.
quotes: Veselago showed that when a material has both permittivity and permeability less than zero, its refractive index would be negative.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to earlier work.

assertions.value: The authors attribute to Pendry the theoretical construction of a lens from an ideal lossless slab with a refractive index of n = −1 that could focus light perfectly and overcome the diffraction limit of a traditional lens.
quotes: Showing, given an ideal lossless slab of material with a refractive index of n = −1 in a medium with equal and opposite refractive index, a lens can be theoretically constructed that could focus light
Crucially such a material could overcome the diffraction limit of a traditional lens.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to earlier work.

papers.title_in_file: HARNESSING CYC TO ANSWER CLINICAL RESEARCHERS’ AD HOC QUERIES
papers.version_note: AI Magazine, Volume 31, Number 3, Fall 2010 (per the text header).
papers.what_it_is: A system paper describing SRA, a Cyc-based interactive system built with Cleveland Clinic for composing and answering clinical researchers' ad hoc queries, with deployment figures and design details.

assertions.value: The authors state that by extending Cyc's ontology and KB approximately 2%, Cycorp and Cleveland Clinic Foundation built a system, SRA, to answer clinical researchers' ad hoc queries.
quotes: By extending Cyc’s ontology and KB approximately 2%, Cycorp and Cleveland Clinic Foundation (CCF) have built a system to answer clinical researchers’ ad hoc queries.
assertions.certainty_reason: Vendor authors describe their own system; no measurement of the 2% figure is given in the body.

assertions.value: The authors report that before SRA about 300 new queries per year were posed and answered in the cardiothoracic surgery, cardiac catheterization and percutaneous coronary intervention domains, most needing 1-10 weeks; in 2010, using SRA, such queries take 5-50 minutes (occasionally several hours) and over 2,000 queries are processed each week.
quotes: Prior to SRA, approximately 300 new queries in those domains had been posed and answered each year, with most queries requiring 1-10 weeks (occasionally several tens of weeks) of real time
in 2010, using SRA, such
queries take 5-50 minutes to produce satisfactory answers (occasionally several hours), and over 2,000 queries are processed each week.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors report deployment figures for their own system; no method for the timing is given.
assertions.reader_inference: The 2,000 per week figure includes persistent bundles re-run on a schedule, as the paper says, so it is not a count of new ad hoc queries.

assertions.value: The authors report that persistent query bundles are re-run each month for internal quality testing and quarterly for external reporting: one bundle of 275 queries produces the data CCF needs to report to STS and a bundle of 256 queries produces the data for ACC.
quotes: persistent bundles of queries in those domains are re-run each month (for internal quality testing purposes) and quarterly (for external third-party reporting purposes)
one bundle of 275 queries produces the procedures and outcomes data CCF needs to report to STS
a bundle of 256 queries produces the data CCF needs to report to ACC (the American College of Cardiology).
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors describe their own deployment.

assertions.value: The authors report that email logs tracking 900 queries over the last few years at CCF show a mean completion time of approximately one month of real time through a two-intermediary process, effectively limiting researchers to about a dozen such queries per year.
quotes: the email logs tracking 900 of these queries over the last few years at CCF show a mean time for this process to complete of approximately one month of real time, effectively limiting researchers to about a dozen such queries per year.
assertions.certainty_reason: One site's email-log measurement reported by the authors; the method is not detailed.

assertions.value: The authors state their aim for SRA is to let physicians pose complex ad hoc questions directly and have them understood and answered in four minutes rather than four weeks.
quotes: Our aim with SRA is to enable physicians to pose their complex ad hoc questions directly, getting them understood and answered in four minutes rather than four weeks.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own design aim in Section 2.

assertions.value: The authors list five AI challenges between the enquirer and an answer: understanding the literal query, understanding the intended query, finding the answer from heterogeneous sources, presenting answers usefully, and failing soft with semantic search.
quotes: Challenge 1: Getting the literal query understood
Challenge 2: Getting the intended query understood.
Challenge 3: Given a complete, unambiguous, logical form of the intended query, finding the answer to that query.
Challenge 4: Present the answers to the physician in a useful fashion.
Challenge 5: In cases where the system would otherwise fail to return an answer, it should “fail soft”
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines its own five challenges in Section 2.

assertions.value: The authors state that the state of the art of natural language parsing cannot reliably parse even short ad hoc queries such as Q1 into a precise, unambiguous logical or database query representation.
quotes: But the state of the art of natural language parsing today cannot reliably parse even shorter ad hoc queries such as Q1 into a precise, unambiguous logical or data base query language representation.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim about the state of the art in 2010, with no supporting evaluation.

assertions.value: The authors state that SPARQL optimization had not yet become available for RDF/OWL triple stores, resulting in queries taking orders of magnitude too long, and that they expect the problem to solve itself in the next five years.
quotes: for which such optimization has not yet become available, resulting in queries taking orders of magnitude too long.
We expect this problem to solve itself in the next five years, as commercial SPARQL optimization catches up with SQL optimization.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim and forecast with no measurement.

assertions.value: The authors state that because accurate parsing of complex medical queries to precise logical representations is beyond the state of the art, SRA's main process is an interactive clarification dialogue; the user selects query fragments, shown as English fill-in-the-blank paraphrases, and tells the system to combine them.
quotes: Since accurate parsing of complex medical queries to precise logical representations is well beyond the state of the art, the main process used is an interactive clarification dialogue between the system and the user
The user highlights the fragments representing parts of the query they had in mind, and tells the system to combine them.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper describes its own workflow in Section 3.1.

assertions.value: The authors state that SRA combines fragments into a single predicate calculus query using the full Cyc KB and inference engine, and that two of the most important decisions are which variables unify and the type and scope of each quantifier.
quotes: SRA brings the entire Cyc knowledge base and inference engine to bear in support of the combination process.
(a) which variables unify with which other variables (i.e., refer to the same thing)? and (b) what is the type of each quantifier (universal or existential) and the scope/nesting of the quantifiers?
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated description of the system's design.

assertions.value: The authors state that constructing hard-wired combination rules for the whole vocabulary would be impractical, and in a footnote that the cardinality of such a set would exceed the number of atoms in the universe.
quotes: it would be impractical5 to construct the corresponding set of hard-wired combination rules.
The cardinality of such a set would exceed the number of atoms in the universe.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim given without derivation.

assertions.value: The authors state that by leveraging the existing Cyc KB, only project specifics needed adding, for example that AVRs are surgical procedures and that pericardial aortic valves are medical implants, and that Cyc has understood the disjointness of event and tangible object collections since 1985.
quotes: it was only necessary to add the specifics for this project: for example, that AVRs are surgical procedures, and that pericardial aortic valves are medical implants6.
Cyc has, since 1985, understood the sort of disjointness between those collections (Lenat and Guha 1989)
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim about reuse without a stated count of assertions added.

assertions.value: The authors report that for the simple query shown in the interface, 1132 answers were found.
quotes: For the simple query shown, 1132 answers were found.
assertions.certainty_reason: A single illustrative query result.

assertions.value: The authors report that the queried data store represented a device as a Model9000IDE rather than a pericardial aortic valve, and that Cyc background knowledge supplied that each 9000IDE is a pericardial aortic valve prosthesis, so that an answer could be justified in natural language.
quotes: The data store being queried did not represent this device as a pericardial aortic valve, but as a Model9000IDE; Cyc provides the background knowledge that each 9000IDE is a pericardial aortic valve prosthesis
assertions.certainty_reason: A single worked example shown by the authors.

assertions.value: The authors report that the Cyc KB holds one rule that adult males have left atrial enlargement if left atrial diameter exceeds 4.2cm, and another that for adult females the cutoff is 3.8cm.
quotes: the Cyc KB has
one rule that says that adult males fall into that category if their left atrial diameter
exceeds 4.2cm, and another rule that says that for adult females the cutoff is 3.8cm.)
assertions.certainty_reason: A domain rule the authors report as encoded, shown as an example; not independently sourced in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that users have a difficult time keeping temporal constraints straight when presented as English phrases and that doing so is much easier when they are also drawn graphically in a Time Graph.
quotes: It turns out that users have a difficult time keeping temporal constraints straight, if they are presented as English phrases; doing so is much easier when they are also drawn graphically.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author observation with no reported user study.

assertions.value: The authors report that they metered SRA's use of Cyc assertions entered before the collaboration began in 2007 and found that hundreds of pre-existing pieces of prior and tacit knowledge were used for each ad hoc query.
quotes: we metered the SRA system’s use of pre-existing Cyc knowledge (that is, assertions entered into Cyc before our collaboration with CCF started in 2007).
hundreds of preexisting pieces of prior and tacit knowledge in Cyc were used for each ad hoc query.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study; no distribution or method detail is given.

assertions.value: The authors state that they avoided the most sophisticated available parsing techniques because they do not produce interpretations consistently and rapidly enough for a predictable user experience, and use a shallower approach based on identifying semantic terms, augmented with a specific parser for relations such as temporal constraints.
quotes: We have therefore avoided the use of the most sophisticated parsing techniques available in the Cyc platform and elsewhere in NLP research
they do not do so consistently enough and rapidly enough for a predictable user experience.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states a design choice and scope of its own system.

assertions.value: The authors report that around 24% of the 126,000 most accessed Wikipedia pages from a typical hour had a corresponding existing Cyc concept, and that term coverage is nearly complete for domains with custom knowledge representation such as cardiothoracic surgery.
quotes: Coverage is already high (around 24% of the 126,000 most accessed Wikipedia pages from a typical hour had a corresponding existing Cyc concept)
term coverage is nearly complete.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical figure from one sample reported by the authors; the sampling method is not described.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper calls 24% 'high'; that is the authors' judgment, not a comparison against a baseline.

assertions.value: The authors report that the SRA sense filter, a decision tree over Cyc ontology classes, was initially trained by automatically tagging and then manually annotating the relevance of concepts found in 29 example query sentences.
quotes: the SRA filter was initially trained, for example, by automatically tagging and then manually annotating the relevance of the concepts found in a mere 29 example query sentences.
assertions.certainty_reason: A training-set size reported by the authors; no accuracy figure is given.
assertions.reader_inference: No filter accuracy is reported in the paper, so the training-set size alone does not show how well the filter works.

assertions.value: The authors state that SRA's expectation-driving assertions for the medical domain were generated manually by knowledge engineers with domain experts, and that for broader applications such expectations could be generated by forward inference.
quotes: SRA’s expectation-driving assertions for the medical domain have been generated manually by knowledge engineers, in consultation with domain experts, to maximize usability
For broader applications, however, and where less control is needed, such expectations can be generated by forward inference.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states how its own assertions were produced.

assertions.value: The authors state that mixed semantic and syntactic templates are used to recognize temporal constructions, for example matching the pattern for an event between two temporal things yields a temporallyBetween-Inclusive formula.
quotes: mixed semantic/syntactic templates are used to recognize and understand temporal constructions.
causes its arguments to be interpreted as (temporallyBetween-Inclusive <arg1> <arg2> <arg3>).
assertions.certainty_reason: Design of the system's own template, stated in Section 3.2.2.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the typical case shown in the query-composition figure Cyc inference eliminates all possible combinations of a new fragment with the existing query but the correct one in a fraction of a second.
quotes: In this surprisingly typical case, it is able to eliminate all possibilities but the correct one in a fraction of a second.
assertions.certainty_reason: A single illustrated case, with no timing table.

assertions.value: The authors state that if two added clauses have descriptions differing only in specificity, such as a surgery and a valve repair, they are assumed to refer to different entities, although it is logically possible they are the same.
quotes: if two clauses are added with descriptions that differ only with respect to specificity (i.e a description of a surgery, and a valve repair), they are assumed to refer to different entities
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states a heuristic of its own system.

assertions.value: The authors state that for variable and column names, 1750 denotesArgInReln assertions exist in the KB, and otherwise the most specific type constraint that can be rendered as a non-plural noun, has not been used elsewhere, and is not more than 30 characters long is used.
quotes: There are 1750 such assertions in the KB
the first one that can be rendered as a non-plural noun, has not been used elsewhere, and is not more than 30 characters long, is used.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own rule in Section 3.2.3.

assertions.value: The authors report that a user search for 'heart attack' returned relevant pages of the Outcomes booklet, which does not contain that term, because Cyc knew it denotes myocardial infarction and that CABG is a common treatment after MI, while avoiding irrelevant pages that a string-based search would include.
quotes: But the Outcomes booklet does not contain that colloquial term anywhere.
relevant “hits” are returned because the Cyc ontology knew that “heart attack” was a denotation for myocardial infarction
allowed it to not retrieve those irrelevant pages even though a string-based search engine would not have understood and would have included those false positives.
assertions.certainty_reason: A single illustrative example; no precision or recall is reported.
assertions.reader_inference: No retrieval accuracy is measured against a keyword baseline, so the claim of fewer false positives rests on one example.

assertions.value: The authors state that fail-soft capabilities were implemented in CAE and applied experimentally to outcome data in end-user search, but have not been integrated deeply into SRA's initial research cohort selection application.
quotes: they have not been integrated deeply into the SRA’s initial research cohort selection application.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the limit of its own system in footnote 4.

assertions.value: The authors report that adding the cardiac catheterization domain involves approximately 500 new concepts and 6500 new assertions, about half of them lexical, tying concepts to standards including Snomed and ICD-9 and -10, and that the other half involve one or more of the preexisting 500,000 concepts in the Cyc ontology.
quotes: The approximately 500 new concepts and 6500 new assertions which are currently being added, for this domain,
About half of the 6500 new assertions for this domain are lexical assertions
preexisting 500,000 concepts in the Cyc ontology
tying it to standards including Snomed and ICD-9 and -10
assertions.certainty_reason: A count the authors report for work in progress, not a completed measurement.

assertions.value: The authors state that initial acquisition of concepts, terminological assertions and medical knowledge assertions for each domain is done top-down, using a reference text for cardiac catheterization a published handbook first, then expanding from a sample of clinical research and clinical queries.
quotes: The initial acquisition of concepts, terminological assertions, and medical knowledge assertions for each domain is done top-down.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own acquisition method.

assertions.value: The authors report being surprised to find empirically that condensing, formatting and exporting answers has been one of the biggest factors affecting whether and to what extent physicians directly use SRA.
quotes: So we were surprised to find that empirically this has been one of the biggest factors affecting whether and to what extent physicians directly use the SRA.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author observation of use; no usage data is given.

assertions.value: The authors state that, at least in the medical domains explored to date, natural language understanding of detailed queries can be performed largely compositionally, building and refining pieces of the query rather than reasoning about the query as a whole.
quotes: natural language understanding for detailed queries, even quite long queries, can – at least in the medical domains explored to date – be performed in a largely compositional fashion
assertions.certainty_reason: An author observation limited to the domains explored.

assertions.value: The authors state as future work: data-driven clinical practice that retrieves treatment options and outcomes for a patient, explicit user and task models, a smarter data entry capability, and weak and strong forms of Cyc-based semantic searching; for the weak form they say success depends on the algorithms developed.
quotes: Clinical Use: Although the SRA has been developed in the context of cohort-selection for clinical outcome studies
Unlike the other SRA extensions we have just described, this one may succeed or fail based more on the algorithms developed for it.

papers.title_in_file: An Invertible All-optical Logic Gate on Chip
papers.what_it_is: An experimental and simulation study of an all-optical gate in a periodically poled thin-film lithium niobate microring, where quantum Zeno blockade driven by sum-frequency generation lets the earlier-arriving pulse act as control and the later one as signal, so the roles invert with a small change in relative delay.

assertions.value: The authors state that they demonstrate an invertible all-optical gate on chip, in which the roles of control and signal are switchable by slightly adjusting their relative arrival time at the gate, based on quantum Zeno blockade driven by sum-frequency generation in a periodic-poled lithium niobate microring resonator.
quotes: We demonstrate an invertible all-optical gate on chip, with the roles of control and signal switchable by slightly adjusting their relative arrival time at the gate.
It is based on quantum Zeno blockade driven by sum-frequency generation in a periodic-poled lithium niobate microring resonator.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical demonstration from one device in one study.

assertions.reader_inference: The measured best delay is 600 ps and the simulated best delay is 500 ps; the paper does not comment on that difference.

assertions.value: The authors report that the simulated signal transmission for the strong-signal case shows ringing of about 0.5 ns duration, which they attribute to the pump pulse tail causing critical coupling rather than blockade; this ringing is not observed in the experiment, and they state that photorefractive, thermo-optic and second-harmonic-generation effects may need to be added to the model, which they leave for future study.
assertions.anchor: Strong Signal and Weak Pump, p.5
quotes: the simulated signal transmission shows a ringing bell oscillation around 0.5 ns duration
Yet, with the detector fast enough, this ringing is not observed in experiment
may need to be added to the current model for a more accurate description of the system dynamics. This will remain a task for the future studies.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper writes 'with the detector fast enough' without giving the detector bandwidth in relation to 0.5 ns; the setup lists a 10 GHz photodetector.

assertions.value: The authors state that their simulations agree well with the experiments, with subtle differences from photorefractive, thermo-optic and second-harmonic-generation effects not captured by the model, and propose MgO doping against photorefractive effects, narrower phase matching against second-harmonic generation, and monitoring the signal at an adjacent period plus tuning the lasers and thermoelectric cooler against thermo-optic effects.
quotes: Our simulation results agree well with the experimental results, with subtle differences coming from side effects not captured by our model
e.g., by addressing PR by MgO2 doping and addressing SHG by narrowing phase matching
To reduce the thermo-optic effect, one can continuously monitor the signal at an adjacent period
assertions.reader_inference: The mitigations are proposals; none is tested in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that modulation performance is not sensitive to pulse length as long as the pulse exceeds the cavity lifetime, and that the MER can be increased by operating in a less over-coupled regime.
quotes: the modulation performance is not sensitive to the pulse length, as long as it exceeds the cavity life-time
Also, the MER can be increased by operating in a less over-coupling regime.
assertions.reader_inference: Only two pulse conditions (10 ns quasi-CW and 2 ns Gaussian signal) were run, and the paper itself says the coupling changed between them, so the pulse-length claim is not isolated by these data.

assertions.value: The authors state that the power consumption for modulation is 12 pJ, and that using shorter pulses closer to the cavity lifetime of 300 ps could reduce the modulation energy to about 1 pJ, though they do not currently have the instrument to create such pulses.
quotes: As of now, the power consumption for modulation is 12 pJ.
By using shorter pulses closer to the cavity lifetime of 300 ps, the modulation energy can be reducted to ∼ 1 pJ, although we currently do not have this instrument to create such pulses.
assertions.reader_inference: A 6 mW peak, 2 ns FWHM pump pulse gives about 12 pJ by simple multiplication (the paper does not show this). The stated 300 ps lifetime is not obviously consistent with Table II: the total decay rates of 9.4 to 10.1 GHz give 1/kappa of about 100 ps if they are energy decay rates in rad/s; the paper does not say how it defines the lifetime. The reduction to about 1 pJ is a projection, not a measurement.

assertions.value: Table I of the paper compares all-optical Zeno effect demonstrations by pump peak power and MER. The MER column reads about 80%, about 51%, about 80% and 85.7% (the last for this work), and the caption says the MER of other works are derived from their modulation results.
assertions.anchor: Table I, p.2 (pump peak power cells too short to quote: [18] 17 W, [19] 680 mW, [20] 180 mW, this work 6 mW)
quotes: Reference Pump Peak Power
The MER of other works are derived from their modulation results.
assertions.reader_inference: The abstract's 'over 30 times' improvement matches 180 mW divided by 6 mW, which is exactly 30 times, against the nearest prior MER (about 80% for reference 20); the introduction's 'over orders of magnitude improvement' matches 17 W versus 6 mW (about 2800 times) but not the other rows. The prior MER values were derived by the authors, not reported by the prior works. The prior work also used different device types and pulse conditions.

assertions.value: The abstract states that with nanosecond pump pulses at 6 mW peak power, 85.7% modulation extinction is observed, achieving an efficiency improvement of over 30 times compared to previous implementations.
quotes: With nanosecond pump pulses at 6 mW peak power, 85.7% modulation extinction is observed, achieving an efficiency improvement of over 30 times compared to previous implementations.
assertions.reader_inference: See Table I: 180 mW to 6 mW is a 30-times ratio in pump peak power, not 'over' 30 times; the comparison is by pump peak power at similar MER.

assertions.value: The authors state that with strong cavity confinement and quasi-phase matching they observe a high MER requiring only milliwatt peak power and picojoule pulse energy, which they describe as over orders of magnitude improvement over the state of the art.
quotes: we observe high modulation extinction ratio (MER) requiring only milliwatt peak power, picojoule pulse energy, corresponding to over orders of magnitude improvement over the state of the art (see Table I below)
assertions.reader_inference: Table I supports a ratio of about 2800 (17 W to 6 mW) against the first reference but about 30 against the nearest one; 'orders of magnitude' is not true for every row.

assertions.value: The authors state that they demonstrate, for the first time, a chip-integrated device for quantum Zeno blockade and efficient all-optical modulation with cascadability and fan-out. The same text lists earlier QZB demonstrations in a thin-film microdisk and in aluminum nitride microrings.
quotes: here we demonstrate, for the first time, a chip-integrated device for QZB and efficient all-optical modulation with cascadability and fanout
a thin-film microdisk [19], and aluminum nitride microrings [20]
assertions.reader_inference: The reader reads the 'first' as qualified by 'efficient ... with cascadability and fanout'; the paper itself lists earlier on-chip QZB demonstrations [19] and [20]. The cascadability and fan-out are shown in this text only as a weak pump modulating a twice-as-strong signal, plus simulations in the Supplemental Materials.

assertions.value: The authors state that once the pump pulses reach the threshold to frustrate the cavity, they can modulate and switch signals of much higher power, and that this feature, which they say originates from quantum Zeno blockade, is essential for scalability, fan-out and absence of critical bias in optical transistors.
assertions.anchor: Strong Signal and Weak Pump, p.4
quotes: When the power of pump pulses reaches the threshold to frustrate the cavity, they can modulate and switch signals of much higher power.
This unique feature, originating from QZB, is essential for scalability, fan out, and absence of critical bias in practical optical transistors.
assertions.reader_inference: The only measured strong-signal point is 4 mW signal against 2 mW pump (a ratio of 2). 'Much higher power' is not tested beyond that ratio in this text.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum Zeno blockade naturally supports superior cascadability, fan-out and absence of critical biasing because the effect transiently changes the cavity condition so the blockade is independent of the signal power level and detailed waveforms, allowing a weaker pump to control a strong signal.
quotes: QZB naturally support superior cascadability, fan out, and absence of critical biasing, as critical for practical optical logic
the blockade effect is independent of the signal’s power level and detailed waveforms
It thus allows a weaker pump to control a strong signal, or the output of one stage to drive multiple subsequent stages.
assertions.reader_inference: The measured MER differs between the 0.2 mW and 4 mW signal cases (49.3% versus 43.3% at 2 mW pump), so the independence is stated for the idealized blockade, not shown as exact in the measurements.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum Zeno blockade is interaction-free and excitation-free, that no excitation of any kind is created because the interaction occurs through the mere potential for a parametric process, and that together these features eliminate phase noise, photon dissipation and quantum state decoherence.
quotes: here no excitation of any kind is created, but the interaction occurs due to the mere potential for a parametric nonlinear optical process (which asymptotically does not occur) [16, 22]
eliminate the occurrence of phase noise, photon dissipation, and quantum state decoherence (e.g., via spontaneous emission) [25]
assertions.reader_inference: This is the authors' framing, supported by their cited work [16, 22, 25]; the experiments here use classical pulses and measure only transmission, so they do not test noise or decoherence.

assertions.value: The authors describe, in a classical-optics picture for a coherent signal, that without a pump the signal builds up in the cavity and destructive interference with the leaked field sends most of it into the cavity, whereas a pump inducing strong sum-frequency or difference-frequency generation quickly converts cavity signal to another wavelength, disrupts the interference, and lets most of the signal continue in the bus waveguide.
quotes: any signal in the cavity will be quickly converted to a different wavelength and effectively lost. This will prohibit its cavity-field building up and thus disrupt the destructive interference.
As a result, the majority of the signal will continue to propagate in the bus waveguide and not enter the cavity [22].

assertions.value: The authors list earlier quantum Zeno blockade demonstrations or analyses in second-order nonlinear (printed χ(2)) waveguides, etalons with sandwiched crystals, whispering-gallery mode cavities, a thin-film microdisk and aluminum nitride microrings, and state that the Zeno effect was first demonstrated in trapped ions in 1990.
quotes: Since its first demonstration in trapped ions in 1990 [5]
quantum Zeno blockade (QZB) was analyzed and demonstrated in nonlinear optical systems, including those of χ(2) waveguides [16, 17]

assertions.value: The authors state that in their Supplemental Materials an all-optical switch is realized by adding a drop port, and that for realistic device parameters and 1 ns pulses a 6 mW signal can be switched by a 2 mW pump with over 90% efficiency, with 65% of the pump surviving the switch so it can switch another signal pulse.
quotes: For realistic device parameters and 1 ns pulses, a 6-mW signal can be switched by a 2-mW pump with over 90% efficiency.
due to interaction-free, 65% of pump survives after the switch, so that it can subsequently switch another signal pulse
assertions.reader_inference: This is a result from the Supplemental Materials, which are not in the text read; the main text gives no measurement of a drop-port device. The reader treats it as a simulated projection.

assertions.value: The authors state that the roles of control and signal are set by which pulse arrives at the cavity first, so conditional logic could be reversed by the relative delay, and that two switches could be cascaded, with the output of one acting as the pump of the next, provided the quasi-phase-matching condition is still met, for example by a frequency converter or a microcavity with multiple phase-matching peaks.
quotes: the roles of control and signal are determined by which arrives at the cavity earlier
two QZB switches can be cascaded to implement a complex operation, with the signal output in one to act as the input pump for the other, as long as the (quasi-)phase matching condition is still met
assertions.reader_inference: No cascaded device was built or measured in this text.

assertions.value: The authors state that the same device shall readily work for single-photon-level quantum signals except for potential Raman scattering, and that raising the intrinsic Q factor to 108 (printed flat; ten to the eighth power), as shown for another laser-written and polished microring, would reduce the required pump power to the single-photon level, opening the door to single-photon anharmonicity and quantum C-NOT gates.
quotes: the same device shall readily work for quantum signals at a single-photon level, except for potential Raman scattering
by improving the intrinsic Q-factor to 108, as demonstrated in a laser-written and chemical and mechanical polished microring [39]
This opens door to singlephoton anharmonicity and quantum C-NOT gates between single photons.
assertions.reader_inference: All experiments in this text use classical pulses at milliwatt peak power; no single-photon or quantum-state measurement is reported, and the Q of 10^8 is a cited result for another device [39], not this chip.

assertions.value: The abstract states that the work demonstrates, for the first time, that optical transistors with cascadability and fan-out are possible with just parametric nonlinear optics.
quotes: This demonstrates, for the first time, that optical transistors with cascadability and fan-out are possible with just parametric nonlinear optics.
assertions.reader_inference: The measurements reported are single-device modulation of one signal by one pump, including a 2-to-1 signal-to-pump power ratio; a cascade of two stages is discussed but not built in the text read.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that they have demonstrated parametric all-optical modulation with high efficiency and presented clear evidence towards practical optical transistor technology, using quantum Zeno blockade in a periodically poled microring in thin-film lithium niobate.
quotes: We have demonstrated parametric all-optical modulation with high efficiency and presented clear evidences towards its uses for practical optical transistor technology.
